A.explanation: With $I = 150 \text{ mA} = 0.15 \text{ A}$ and $R = 0.24 \text{ k}\Omega = 240 \text{ }\Omega$, $IR = 36 \text{ V}$, not $3.6 \text{ V}$.

B.explanation: With $I = 15 \text{ mA} = 0.015 \text{ A}$ and $R = 2.4 \text{ k}\Omega = 2400 \text{ }\Omega$, $IR = 36 \text{ V}$, not $3.6 \text{ V}$.

C.explanation: With $I = 1.5 \text{ mA} = 0.0015 \text{ A}$ and $R = 0.24 \text{ M}\Omega = 240000 \text{ }\Omega$, $IR = 360 \text{ V}$, not $3.6 \text{ V}$.

D.explanation: With $I = 15 \text{ }\mu\text{A} = 15 \times 10^{-6} \text{ A}$ and $R = 240 \text{ k}\Omega = 240 \times 10^{3} \text{ }\Omega$, $IR = 3.6 \text{ V}$, matching the voltmeter.

hints: Notice the voltmeter reading of $3.6 \text{ V}$ across the resistor means the product of the listed current and resistance must equal $3.6 \text{ V}$.
Recall $V = IR$ for the resistor, so convert each current in $\text{mA}$ or $\mu\text{A}$ to $\text{A}$ and each resistance in $\text{k}\Omega$ or $\text{M}\Omega$ to $\Omega$ before multiplying.

Compare powers of ten carefully: $\text{mA}$ with $\text{k}\Omega$ and $\mu\text{A}$ with $\text{k}\Omega$ shift the product by factors of 10, so check which pair gives $3.6$ rather than $36$ or $360$.
walkthrough: The voltmeter measures the potential difference across the resistor, so $V = 3.6 \text{ V}$ must satisfy $V = IR$ for the correct current $I$ and resistance $R$.

Convert prefixes to base units: $1 \text{ mA} = 10^{-3} \text{ A}$, $1 \text{ }\mu\text{A} = 10^{-6} \text{ A}$, $1 \text{ k}\Omega = 10^{3} \text{ }\Omega$ and $1 \text{ M}\Omega = 10^{6} \text{ }\Omega$.
Test the products: option A gives $0.15 \text{ A} \times 240 \text{ }\Omega = 36 \text{ V}$ and option B gives $0.015 \text{ A} \times 2400 \text{ }\Omega = 36 \text{ V}$.
Option C gives $0.0015 \text{ A} \times 240000 \text{ }\Omega = 360 \text{ V}$, which is far too large.
For the remaining pair, $I = 15 \text{ }\mu\text{A} = 15 \times 10^{-6} \text{ A}$ and $R = 240 \text{ k}\Omega = 240 \times 10^{3} \text{ }\Omega$.
Then $V = IR = (15 \times 10^{-6}) \times (240 \times 10^{3}) = 3600 \times 10^{-3} \text{ V} = 3.6 \text{ V}$, with correct volts as $\text{A} \times \Omega$. This is option D.
